Moral Foundations Theory is a framework that separates human morality into the following categories:

  - Care/Harm: related to our long evolution as mammals with attachment systems
    and an ability to feel (and dislike) the pain of others. It underlies the
    virtues of kindness, gentleness, and nurturance.

  - Loyalty/Betrayal: related to our long history as tribal creatures able to
    form shifting coalitions. It is active anytime people feel that it is "one
    for all and all for one." It underlies the virtues of patriotism and
    self-sacrifice for the group.

  - Authority/Subversion: shaped by our long primate history of hierarchical
    social interactions. It underlies virtues of leadership and followership,
    including deference to prestigious authority figures and respect for
    traditions.

  - Sanctity/Purity: shaped by the psychology of disgust and contamination. It
    underlies notions of striving to live in an elevated, less carnal, more
    noble, and more "natural" way (often present in religious narratives). This
    foundation underlies the widespread idea that the body is a temple that can
    be desecrated by immoral activities and contaminants (an idea not unique to
    religious traditions). It underlies the virtues of self-discipline,
    self-improvement, naturalness, and spirituality.

  - Equality: related to our intuitions about equal treatment and equal outcome
    for individuals.

  - Proportionality: related to our intuitions about individuals getting
    rewarded in proportion to their merit or contribution.

Every category has a bidirectional nature. For example:

One person's sensitivity to the Care/Harm foundation may lead them to support high levels of immigration from poorer nations, to reduce the suffering of those who migrate. Whereas another person's sensitivity to the very same foundation may lead them to oppose those levels, because they believe it could lead to people they care about being harmed.

# Labour Party Manifesto 2024: Summary

## Overview and Core Approach

The Labour Party's 2024 manifesto presents a plan centered on five national missions: economic growth, clean energy, crime reduction, expanding opportunity, and NHS reform. The document emphasizes fiscal responsibility, with commitments to balance day-to-day spending with revenues and reduce debt as a share of the economy.

## Economic Policy

Labour proposes establishing an Industrial Strategy Council to guide long-term economic planning across sectors including financial services, automotive, life sciences, and creative industries. A National Wealth Fund would receive £7.3 billion to invest in ports, gigafactories, steel, carbon capture, and green hydrogen production.

The party commits to capping corporation tax at 25%, maintaining full expensing for capital investment, and reforming business rates. Planning reform features prominently, with targets of 1.5 million new homes over the parliament, including restoration of mandatory housing targets and strategic greenbelt release.

Devolution would expand through new powers for combined authorities over transport, skills, housing, and employment support. Local Growth Plans would be developed with employers and educational institutions.

## Energy and Environment

The manifesto targets clean electricity by 2030 through doubling onshore wind, tripling solar, and quadrupling offshore wind. Great British Energy, a publicly-owned company headquartered in Scotland, would receive £8.3 billion in capital.

On North Sea oil and gas, Labour would not revoke existing licenses but would cease issuing new exploration licenses. The windfall tax on energy companies would be extended and increased. A Warm Homes Plan would invest £6.6 billion to upgrade five million homes.

## Public Services

NHS reforms include 40,000 additional weekly appointments, doubling CT and MRI scanners, recruiting 8,500 mental health staff, and establishing specialist rape units in every police force. The party would bring rail services into public ownership as contracts expire.

Education proposals include 6,500 new teachers funded by ending VAT exemptions for private schools, free breakfast clubs in primary schools, and 3,000 new nurseries in primary school buildings. A curriculum review would be conducted.

## Immigration and Security

A Border Security Command would replace the Rwanda scheme, with counter-terrorism-style powers to target smuggling networks. The party would seek a security agreement with the EU for intelligence sharing. Additional caseworkers would address asylum backlogs, and a returns unit with 1,000 staff would expedite removals.

Defence commitments include maintaining the nuclear deterrent, NATO membership, and conducting a Strategic Defence Review with a path to 2.5% GDP spending.

## Constitutional Reform

Proposed changes include removing hereditary peers from the House of Lords, introducing mandatory retirement at 80 for peers, extending voting rights to 16-17 year olds, and establishing an Ethics and Integrity Commission. The party would reset relationships with devolved governments through a new Council of the Nations and Regions.

## Funding

Revenue measures include closing non-dom tax status loopholes, ending private equity carried interest treatment as capital gains, extending energy windfall taxes, and modernizing HMRC enforcement. Spending efficiencies would come from halving consultancy costs, police collaboration programs, and ending asylum hotel use.

# Conservative Party Manifesto 2024: Summary

## Economic Policy

The manifesto outlines plans to reduce employee National Insurance from 12% to 6% by April 2027, representing a £1,350 annual reduction for average earners. Self-employed individuals would see their main National Insurance rate abolished entirely. The party commits to maintaining fiscal rules requiring public sector net debt to fall and borrowing to remain below 3% of GDP.

Business support includes maintaining corporation tax rates, extending "full expensing" to leasing when conditions allow, and a ten-point plan for SMEs covering business rates relief, VAT threshold reviews, and improved access to finance.

## Taxation and Pensions

The "Triple Lock Plus" would ensure State Pensions rise annually by the highest of inflation, earnings, or 2.5%, while introducing a new age-related personal allowance to prevent pensioners being drawn into income tax. Child Benefit reforms would move to a household-based system, with withdrawal beginning at £120,000 combined income.

## Immigration

Proposals include a legally binding annual cap on migration covering work and family visas, with Parliament voting on levels each year. The Rwanda removal scheme would continue, alongside reforms to asylum rules and increased visa fees. Health checks for migrants would be introduced, with potential Immigration Health Surcharge increases.

## Defence and Security

Defence spending would increase to 2.5% of GDP by 2030, with £10 billion invested in munitions production. Plans include continued Ukraine support, nuclear deterrent modernisation, and a National Defence and Resilience Plan.

## Healthcare

NHS spending would increase above inflation annually, with commitments to recruit 92,000 additional nurses and 28,000 doctors. Pharmacy First expansion, 250 new or modernised GP surgeries, and 50 Community Diagnostic Centres are planned. Social care cost caps would be implemented from October 2025.

## Housing

The target is 1.6 million new homes, achieved through brownfield development fast-tracking, planning reforms, and abolishing EU nutrient neutrality rules. First-time buyers would benefit from permanent Stamp Duty relief up to £425,000 and a new Help to Buy scheme.

## Education and Skills

Proposals include mandatory National Service for 18-year-olds (military or civic), 100,000 new apprenticeships funded by closing underperforming university courses, and the Advanced British Standard for 16-19 education. Mobile phones would be banned during school hours.

## Energy and Environment

Annual oil and gas licensing rounds would continue, alongside trebling offshore wind capacity and building Small Modular Reactors. Green levies on household bills would be kept lower than 2023 levels. Net zero by 2050 remains the target.

## Transport

£36 billion from HS2 savings would fund regional transport improvements, including £8.3 billion for road maintenance. The £2 bus fare cap would continue throughout the Parliament. Measures would prevent road pricing and reverse London's ULEZ expansion.

## Welfare Reform

Plans include reforming disability benefits assessment, tightening work capability assessments, and introducing stricter sanctions for those refusing suitable employment after 12 months. Projected savings total £12 billion annually.
